summary.text: 水 pictures flowing water as a current with droplets beside it. Its common meaning is “water.”

formation.text: This is a whole-character pictograph. In the described oracle forms, a central stroke represents the current and side marks represent droplets; these form one picture, not separate character components. A Han-era explanation adds a cosmological interpretation distinct from this graphic construction.

components.text: The whole character pictures flowing water: its central stroke represents the current and its side marks droplets. Their number varies in early forms; they are not separate character components.

history.text: Oracle forms vary in their side marks. Bronze and Warring States forms are described as retaining the flowing-water picture. The selected oracle and Western Zhou bronze glyphs illustrate script forms; they do not establish a sequence of graphic changes.
A Han-era account glosses 水 as “level” and explains the character through the cosmology of its time. This is a historical explanation of the graph, separate from its pictorial construction.

uncertainties.text: Proposals for the spoken word’s earlier pronunciation and possible connections to other languages differ. They concern the word’s pronunciation, not a sound component in the graph.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone examples; individual dates unresolved
senses.text: Reported Shang oracle-bone examples use 水 for water or flooding. The examples are not individually dated, so they do not establish that this is the earliest attested sense.
The common current meaning is “water.” Other recorded glosses include liquid, lotion, and juice, but their chronology is not established.

A bronze inscription is reported to use 水 to write the different word 乞, “request.” This is proposed graph borrowing: the sign was reused because the words may have sounded alike, not because water developed the meaning “request.” Their historical sound match is unconfirmed.
One reported oracle-bone use is read as a verb involving either leveling ground with water or washing a temple. Its reading and any connection to the noun “water” remain unresolved.

developments.text: The graph is reported to have been reused for 乞, “request,” on the proposed basis that the words sounded alike or similarly. The old spoken name of the pictured water and a historical comparison between the words’ pronunciations are not established.

limitations.text: The oracle examples are not individually dated here. Whether the disputed verbal use is related to the noun “water” is unresolved.
The proposed sound-based explanation for writing 乞 with 水 lacks a confirmed historical comparison of their pronunciations.
水準 is reported in compounds meaning a leveling instrument and, later, an abstract “standard” or “level.” These compound meanings are not separate senses of 水; the stages are undated here.

overview.text: 水 pictures flowing water, with a central current and marks for droplets. Its common meaning is “water.”

components.text: Together, the central line and side marks picture a current and its droplets.
